title: A lattice algorithm found a pulsar hidden in sparse gamma rays
freshness: Peer-reviewed Physical Review Letters article published November 19, 2026; preferred 15-day search window.
excerpt: A new search method uncovered PSR J1622-7204, a neutron star that spins 261 times each second, in 15 years of sparse gamma-ray data. By turning the missing rotations between photons into a geometry problem, the researchers cut a previously unsuccessful search from centuries of processor time to about ten hours.
whyItMatters: Many gamma-ray pulsars may already be present in telescope archives but remain hidden because conventional searches require too much computing. A faster method could enlarge the pulsar census and eventually reveal tight binary systems useful for studying neutron stars and gravity.
whatToExploreNext: How can the arrival times of a few photons reveal a neutron star's rotation rate?

sources.label: Gamma-Ray Pulsar Discovery Using a Lattice-Based Method

body:
## A clock hidden in a handful of photons

A neutron star in the southern sky spins 261 times every second, yet NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope records only about one of its photons for every 100 million rotations. Researchers have now found that hidden clock. The new pulsar, PSR J1622-7204, emerged from 15 years of Fermi data after a search method recast the problem as geometry.

A pulsar is the compact remnant left when a massive star collapses. Its strong magnetic field channels particles into beams of radiation. If a beam sweeps across Earth as the star rotates, telescopes see a repeating pulse, much like the flash of a lighthouse. At radio wavelengths, those flashes can be plentiful. Gamma-ray photons are much rarer, so the rhythm is buried beneath long gaps.

Finding that rhythm requires testing a pulsar's sky position, spin rate and gradual slowdown. The motion of Fermi around Earth, and Earth around the Sun, also changes photon arrival times slightly. A conventional search must explore an enormous number of possible combinations. An earlier semicoherent search for this source failed after using computing time equivalent to roughly 600 years on one processor core.

## Turning missing rotations into geometry

The new method begins with a simple fact: between any two photons from the pulsar, the star must complete a whole number of rotations. The difficulty is that astronomers do not know that number. It could be millions or billions.

The researchers represented possible rotation counts as points in a high-dimensional lattice, a regular mathematical grid. Each point corresponds to one proposed set of whole-number counts between photon arrivals. A correct set must agree with one spin frequency and its slow change through time. Wrong guesses leave larger fractional mismatches. Algorithms developed to find short vectors in lattices can search these possibilities far more efficiently than checking them one by one.

For the successful discovery, the team ran 20 trials, each using a slightly different selection of 80 photons. One trial found the pulsar's timing pattern. The paper reports about ten CPU hours in total, while the accompanying institute account describes 100 minutes of elapsed work from 20 five-minute single-core runs. Those figures describe different ways of counting the computation, but both show the same large gain over the earlier search.

The team also measured the star's gradual slowdown. Their timing solution implies that after about 100 million years it would make roughly five fewer rotations per second than it does now. PSR J1622-7204 appears to be isolated, with no detected companion in this analysis.

## One discovery, with a wider possibility

What was measured is a coherent 261-hertz pulse pattern in archival gamma-ray data and the rate at which that pattern changes. The broader promise is still a forecast. The authors argue that the method may make searches for binary gamma-ray pulsars practical even when the companion's orbit is not already known. Such systems can provide sensitive tests of neutron-star physics and gravity.

The successful run was also fortunate. The researchers estimate that about 300 randomized trials would be needed for a 95 percent chance of finding this pulsar, rather than the 20 they happened to use. Even with that caveat, the result shows that sparse photons need not make a pulsar computationally invisible. Better mathematics can expose a signal that was already waiting in the archive.
